title: Alhambra color palettes: historical pigments from the Nasrid dynasty
text: reigns Yusuf Muhammad V, Nasrid color palette reached full expression prominent use gold throughout palace complex. Artisans developed complex polychrome designs featuring sophisticated color modulation techniques created three-dimensional illusions flat surfaces. period also saw introduction royal purple derived kermes murex, marking height Nasrid decorative arts.

title: Alhambra color palettes: historical pigments from the Nasrid dynasty

title: Chameleon color palettes: nature's masters of chromatic adaptation
text: Chameleons (family Chamaeleonidae) renowned remarkable ability change color, capacity fascinated naturalists since antiquity. Contrary popular belief, chameleons change color primarily camouflage; rather, color change serves functions thermoregulation, communication, social signaling (Stuart-Fox & Moussalli (2009)). mechanism underlying color change involves specialized cells called chromatophores arranged layers beneath transparent epidermis. uppermost layer contains xanthophores (yellow pigments) erythrophores (red pigments), deeper layers contain iridophores guanine nanocrystals reflect light, melanophores containing dark melanin. adjusting spacing nanocrystals iridophore layer, chameleons can shift reflecting short wavelengths (blue) long wavelengths (red), overlying yellow pigments producing characteristic green coloration combined blue reflectance (Teyssier et al. (2015)). koloRo includes 20 palettes based documented coloration patterns chameleon species three continents, derived scientific literature, field guides, natural history documentation.

text: Color vision deficiency (CVD), commonly called “color blindness,” affects approximately 8% males 0.5% females Northern European descent. Understanding CVD types essential creating accessible visualizations.

title: Scientific color palettes: perceptually uniform colormaps for oceanography and earth sciences
text: decades, “rainbow” “jet” colormap default choice scientific visualization. However, research demonstrated rainbow colormaps fundamentally flawed scientific communication (Borland & Taylor (2007); Light & Bartlein (2004)): Non-uniform perceptual lightness: human visual system perceives brightness changes non-linearly across hues. Yellow appears much brighter blue equal saturation, creating artificial “bands” continuous data. Loss information: Crameri et al. (2020) showed rainbow colormaps can hide 7% data features compared perceptually uniform alternatives. Colorblind inaccessibility: Rainbow colormaps particularly problematic ~8% males red-green color vision deficiency (Wong (2011)). False boundaries: Abrupt perceptual transitions (e.g., cyan--green) create apparent boundaries data none exist.

code: # Simulated SST data (realistic range: -2 to 30°C) set.seed(42) lon <- seq(-180, 180, length.out = 100) lat <- seq(-90, 90, length.out = 50) sst_grid <- expand.grid(lon = lon, lat = lat)  # Temperature decreases with latitude, with some noise sst_grid$sst <- 28 - abs(sst_grid$lat) * 0.35 +   5 * sin(sst_grid$lon * pi / 180) * cos(sst_grid$lat * pi / 90) +   rnorm(nrow(sst_grid), sd = 1) sst_grid$sst <- pmax(-2, pmin(32, sst_grid$sst))  ggplot(sst_grid, aes(lon, lat, fill = sst)) +   geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +   scale_fill_koloro_c("batlow") +   coord_fixed(expand = FALSE) +   labs(     title = "Sea surface temperature (simulated)",     subtitle = "Using batlow colormap",     x = "Longitude",     y = "Latitude",     fill = "SST (\u00B0C)"   ) +   theme_minimal() +   theme(     panel.grid = element_blank(),     legend.position = "bottom",     legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm")   )

text: Ocean depth data benefits palettes transition smoothly shallow (light) deep (dark):
code: # Simulated bathymetry set.seed(123) bathy_grid <- expand.grid(   x = seq(0, 100, length.out = 80),   y = seq(0, 60, length.out = 48) )  # Create realistic continental shelf and deep ocean bathy_grid$depth <- with(bathy_grid, {   shelf <- ifelse(x < 20, -50 - x * 5, -150)   slope <- ifelse(x >= 20 & x < 40, -150 - (x - 20) * 100, shelf)   deep <- ifelse(x >= 40, -2000 - 500 * sin((x - 40) * pi / 60), slope)   deep + rnorm(length(deep), sd = 100) })  ggplot(bathy_grid, aes(x, y, fill = depth)) +   geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +   scale_fill_koloro_c("deep_sea", direction = -1) +   coord_fixed(expand = FALSE) +   labs(     title = "Bathymetric profile (simulated)",     subtitle = "Continental shelf to abyssal plain",     x = "Distance from coast (km)",     y = "Along-shore distance (km)",     fill = "Depth (m)"   ) +   theme_minimal() +   theme(     panel.grid = element_blank(),     legend.position = "right"   )

code: # Simulated sea surface temperature (SST) data set.seed(123) lon <- seq(-180, 180, length.out = 50) lat <- seq(-60, 60, length.out = 30) sst_grid <- expand.grid(lon = lon, lat = lat)  # Temperature gradient with latitude and some spatial variation sst_grid$sst <- 28 - 0.4 * abs(sst_grid$lat) +   2 * sin(sst_grid$lon * pi / 60) * cos(sst_grid$lat * pi / 40) +   rnorm(nrow(sst_grid), 0, 1.5)  ggplot(sst_grid, aes(lon, lat, fill = sst)) +   geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +   scale_fill_koloro_c("batlow", name = "SST (\u00B0C)") +   labs(     title = "Sea surface temperature with Batlow palette",     subtitle = "Perceptually uniform colormap for scientific visualization",     x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude"   ) +   coord_fixed(ratio = 1.5) +   theme_minimal() +   theme(     plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),     legend.position = "right"   ) # Temperature anomaly data sst_grid$anomaly <- sst_grid$sst - mean(sst_grid$sst)  ggplot(sst_grid, aes(lon, lat, fill = anomaly)) +   geom_raster(interpolate = TRUE) +   scale_fill_koloro_div("vik", midpoint = 0, name = "Anomaly (\u00B0C)") +   labs(     title = "SST anomalies with Vik diverging palette",     x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude"   ) +   coord_fixed(ratio = 1.5) +   theme_minimal()

Cultural palettes (20+): Japanese (edo, zen, sakura), Persian (miniature, carpet, garden), Chinese (imperial, ink, jade, porcelain), Indian (holi, spice, monsoon), African, Nordic, Mediterranean traditions. Artistic movement palettes (15+): Historical movements (impressionist, renaissance, baroque, rococo) modern styles (art_deco, bauhaus, pop_art, street_art, minimalist).
